questions.prompt: What is Chapter 12's main claim about human-machine systems?
choices: The strongest systems often come from complementarity rather than simple replacement
Technology succeeds only when people disappear from the workflow entirely
Humans and machines should always do the same tasks together

explanation.gentle: The chapter says strong systems often come from combining different strengths well.
explanation.direct: Its main claim is that complementarity is often stronger than simple replacement.
explanation.competitive: The real win is the split, not the wipeout.

questions.prompt: Why is simple replacement too weak as an explanation in this chapter?
choices: Because people always outperform computers
Because not all tasks in a workflow are the same kind of task
Because technology should never change work roles

explanation.gentle: The chapter says different parts of the workflow involve different strengths.
explanation.direct: Replacement is too simple because scan-heavy work and judgment-heavy work are not the same thing.
explanation.competitive: You cannot delete the human cleanly if the tasks are not all one category.

questions.prompt: What makes complementarity stronger than vague “humans still matter” talk?
choices: It keeps people in the system for sentimental reasons
It treats technology as weaker than human judgment in every case
It divides work concretely around different strengths

explanation.gentle: The chapter ties complementarity to a real split of work rather than to general reassurance.
explanation.direct: Its mechanism is concrete division of labor, not sentiment.
explanation.competitive: Complementarity wins by assigning the work honestly.

questions.prompt: Maya's system scans a huge flagged-cases list, and Maya decides which cases actually matter. What lesson fits best?
choices: A machine can handle pattern-heavy work while a person handles judgment-heavy work
The machine should replace Maya completely next
The system works only because Maya ignores the software

explanation.gentle: The chapter says the split between scan work and judgment work can make the system stronger.
explanation.direct: Maya's workflow shows complementarity in practical form.

questions.prompt: Why should Rowan's seminar team map task categories before deciding what to automate?
choices: Because full automation is always a mistake
Because divided strengths matter more than an all-or-nothing slogan
Because machines cannot do any useful work

explanation.gentle: The team needs to separate pattern-heavy work from judgment-heavy work first.
explanation.direct: The chapter says task categories should guide the split, not automation rhetoric alone.
explanation.competitive: Classify the work before you declare victory.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main point about divided strengths?
choices: Computers and people should mostly do the same work together
Different strengths can be combined into a stronger system
People matter only when machines are not available

explanation.gentle: The chapter says the best system often comes from combining different kinds of strength.
explanation.direct: Divided strengths matter because complementarity can improve the whole workflow.
explanation.competitive: The stronger system comes from the split.

questions.prompt: Why does system design matter so much in Chapter 12?
choices: Because the workflow gets stronger only if the work is divided well
Because future prophecy is more useful than present workflow design
Because technology should avoid changing any human role

explanation.gentle: The chapter says the split of work is what makes the system useful or weak.
explanation.direct: System design matters because complementarity depends on assigning the right work to the right side.
explanation.competitive: The workflow wins or loses on the split.

questions.prompt: Kira redesigns her process so the tool sorts and scans while she keeps the harder review decisions. What is she doing?
choices: Proving that machines always lose to humans
Using complementarity to redesign the workflow around divided strengths
Turning the tool into a decorative extra

explanation.gentle: Kira is giving the tool and the person different jobs based on their strengths.
explanation.direct: This is augmentation as workflow redesign rather than as vague reassurance.
explanation.competitive: She is building the split on purpose.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 12 connect augmentation and business usefulness?
choices: Useful augmentation comes from a better division of labor, not from sentimental comfort
Augmentation matters only because it sounds more humane than replacement
Business usefulness depends on keeping machines away from judgment entirely

explanation.gentle: The chapter says augmentation matters when it improves how the work is actually done.
explanation.direct: Business usefulness comes from a stronger workflow split rather than from softer rhetoric.
explanation.competitive: A sharper system beats a nicer story.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 12 prepare the next chapter?
choices: It asks why big technology bets can still fail when timing and business design are wrong
It concludes that any ambitious technology system will succeed if complementarity exists
It returns from workflow design to generic labor prophecy

explanation.gentle: The next chapter asks why technology bets can still go wrong despite real technical ambition.
explanation.direct: The bridge moves from complementarity to failure in timing, scale, and business design.
explanation.competitive: The next question is why the bet still blows up.
